description: We are a team from Pakistan participating in the Hyderabad virtual Local Event. We aim to build a practical crop-rotation decision-support prototype using NASA Earth observations, local soil information, crop characteristics, and farmer priorities. Our interests include software development, AI, data analysis, and web applications. We welcome teammates with agriculture/soil science, GIS, Earth science, data visualization, UI/UX, and science communication skills.
summary: Indus CropWise AI is a web-based decision-support prototype developed by Team IndusAstra for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Field Shift. It helps farmers and agricultural learners in the Indus region explore crop-rotation options by combining NASA POWER daily climate information with user-entered farm context, a six-crop catalogue, and farmer-selected priorities. The application displays temperature, precipitation, and humidity indicators, then compares candidate crop sequences using transparent, rule-based scores for water fit, climate fit, soil/rotation diversity, and farmer priority fit. Each comparison includes explanations and warnings when information is missing. The prototype is intended for exploration and education; it is not a validated agronomic model and does not guarantee yield, profit, soil improvement, or water savings.
details:
Indus CropWise AI addresses the Field Shift challenge by turning climate information and farm context into an understandable crop-rotation comparison. A user starts with a demonstration point near Hyderabad, Sindh, or enters other coordinates. The application retrieves daily temperature, maximum and minimum temperature, corrected precipitation and relative humidity from the NASA POWER Daily Point API (Agroclimatology community). Users can inspect the data period, units and source status. The user then enters available farm information such as soil type, pH if known, salinity status, drainage and irrigation availability, and selects priorities such as water saving, soil health, income or food security.

A six-crop catalogue covers wheat, cotton, rice, maize, chickpea and mung bean. Four predefined example rotations and a custom sequence can be explored. The comparison uses four transparent components: Water Fit (30%), Climate Fit (25%), Soil/Rotation Diversity (25%) and Farmer Priority Fit (20%). If a component cannot be computed because required information is missing, the app shows a warning and re-normalizes the remaining weights. Users can inspect component explanations and trade-offs rather than receiving an unexplained single recommendation.

In the current version, irrigation availability and salinity directly influence scoring. Soil texture, pH, drainage and organic matter are collected as context but are not all incorporated into the present scoring formula. Some farmer-priority tags, including income, are illustrative comparisons and are not market prices or validated economic estimates. The application is a deterministic, rule-based educational prototype, not a trained machine-learning model or field-validated agronomy system. Results should be checked with local soil tests and qualified agricultural experts before being used for real farming decisions.
